feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The care workforce is moving out of buildings and into homes, and the per-facility records families use to judge a building were refreshed on the same calendar. BLS puts nursing care facilities employment at 1,590.20 thousands of jobs in August 2026, up 2.1% year over year, while home health care services employment reached 1,896.40 thousands of jobs, up 5.0%, and continuing care retirement communities and assisted living reached 1,026.90 thousands of jobs, up 1.4%. Four sources land on this same long-term care story independently, and CMS refreshed Provider Information, Health Deficiencies, Penalties, Ownership and Survey Summary on 08/01/26, files that carry per-facility staffing measures and three years of citations and fines for the period the labor series describes. No monitored publisher matched the nursing care facilities or home health employment figures.

**Why it matters:** Facility-based care is competing for workers against a home-based sector growing more than twice as fast and paying more: average hourly earnings for July 2026 run $28.04 in home health against $25.65 in assisted living and CCRCs. A family comparing two nursing homes can pull staffing, citations and fines for each one out of the refreshed files; what no single facility record shows is that the sector added workers at 2.1% while the alternative added them at 5.0%, which is the pressure sitting behind every staffing line on a Five-Star profile. The CMS side of this is refreshed reference data rather than a new finding, so the piece rests its argument on the employment and earnings series and uses the files to make it concrete facility by facility.

**Why pitch this now:** August 2026 is the current month on all three employment series and July 2026 on both earnings series, so the year-over-year gap between facility and home-based hiring is as fresh as it gets. The nursing home citation, penalty and survey files carry an 08/01/26 refresh and cover the last three years, which means the facility-level record and the national labor picture describe the same window this month and will drift apart next.

**Angle:** Whether the staffing that a nursing home's public quality record is measured on can hold while home-based care hires faster and pays more, told through the August payroll counts and the refreshed facility files. Working title: "Where the Aides Went." For skilled nursing operators and administrators, and for the families reading their star ratings.

**Potential headlines:**
- Nursing homes are adding staff at less than half the rate of home health
- What three years of citations and fines say about the home you are considering
- The care workforce is growing fastest inside people's houses

**Potential outlets:**
- **McKnight's Long-Term Care News** — its skilled nursing readers manage against staffing and reimbursement numbers weekly, and the August employment series is their own sector's payroll count.
- **Skilled Nursing News** — an operations, finance and M&A readership can pair the refreshed Ownership and Facility Affiliation files with 2.1% headcount growth.
- **Provider Magazine** — covers nursing facilities and assisted living together, which is exactly where the 1.4% growth and $25.65 hourly earnings figure lands.
- **Kiplinger** — readers comparing facilities and long-term care costs need the per-facility staffing and penalty records translated into what to look up before signing.

Continuing care retirement communities and assisted living employed 1,026.90 thousands, up 1.4%. I want to write about 1,200 words on what that divergence does to facility staffing, using the BLS series alongside the CMS files refreshed 08/01/26: Provider Information, which carries the staffing measures behind the Five-Star Rating System, plus Health Deficiencies, Penalties, Ownership and Survey Summary, each covering the last three years. Average hourly earnings for July 2026 run $28.04 in home health against $25.65 in assisted living and CCRCs, which gives the piece its second thread. The finished story would say whether payroll growth in skilled nursing is keeping pace with the staffing its public quality record is judged on, state by state where the files allow. McKnight's is where operators go for staffing and reimbursement data, and this is their own payroll count.
